deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
Front: Why does SG parliament only have 1 house?
Back:
- SG too small
- separate chambers would be too divisive
- upper chamber might become the mouthpiece of a minority party
- second chamber would be severely critcised if it thwarted the will of the majority, as expressed through elected representatives
- difficulties in finding suitable candidates

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
Front: How do candidates become part of Parliament?
Back:
Singapore’s legislature consisted of representatives voted
into office by popular vote under the single plurality first past the post
system.

Person securing the most number of votes in Constituency thus declared
to become members of parliament

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
Back:
■ SG citizen

■ At least 21 years old

■ Resident of SG at the time of
nomination

■ Of sound mind and able to
actively take part in debate in Parliament

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
Back:
- Legislative power vested in parliament - makes bills, amendments to law i.e. govern all aspects of lives
- debates the govt budget of respective ministries. ability to scrutinise, clarify and challenge govt policies

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
Back:
Very strict
- no one votes against govt lines, members of a particular party will loyally vote according to the party's dictates
- members who vote against their own party's policies etc will be dealt with by the party's disciplinarian, the whip. he may lose his party membership and hence his seat in Parliament

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
Front: Why are private members' bills extremely rare?
Back:
■ As ruling PAP has continuously been in
power since 1959, no real opportunity for its backbenches to introduce new
legislation of their own since the party is already in power

■ At both formulation and actual law-making
stages, MPs assume a more muted and passive role

■ MPs lack legislative initiative and almost
all legislation comes from the Cabinet acting on its own initiative or on the
advice of senior civil servants

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
Front: Is the Whip imposed for private members' bills?
Back: No, can speak more freely and in good conscience

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
Front: What are the purposes of the GRC?
Back:
- ensure minority representation in parliament
- efficiently manage SG's public housing estates

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
Front: What are the weaknesses of the GRC scheme?
Back:
- constant enlargement of GRCs and shifting of political boundaries made it very difficult for opposition parties to get a foothold in GEs. ethnic minority and 3 to 6 member requirement made it difficult for opposition parties to contest due to their small size
- Electoral boundaries commission, which report directly to the PM's ofice, draws the constituency boundaries before a GE (gerrymandering)
- Most opposition parties lacked recognisable
personalities to helm their GRC teams, unlike the PAP, who strategically placed
well-known cabinet ministers as leaders of their GRC teams

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
Back:
- NCMP seats offered to the top losers in GE
- picked from parties whose members were not members of govt
- increased from 3 to 6 to 9
- now max 12 NCMPs can be picked to set a minimum number of opp MPs
- 1st NCMP after 1984 GE: Dr Lee Siew Choh of WP

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
Back:
From 1984 to 2017, NCMPs can only debate on parliamentary issues. Prohibited from voting on constitutional amendments, supply bills and motions of confidence on the govt

In 2016, Article 38 of the constitution was amended to allow NCMPs to vote on all bills after 2017. Same voting rights as MPs as NCMP have as much mandate as MPs

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
Back:
- offer an alternative voice in the parliament through opp party members that are not elected
- keep govt on its toes
- quell Singaporeans' desire to elect an alternative party into power

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
Back:
- Lacked legitimacy
- 3/99 seats for NCMPs too small to make a difference
- Public likened it to tokenism
- NCMPs get no support from parliament to engage assistance to help them in their work

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
Back: Can participate in all debates but cannot vote on constitutional amendments, supply bills and motions of confidence on the govt

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
Back:
Include alternative, non-partisan voices in parliament which could add to the variety of
view during parliamentary debate and raise the tenure of debate in the House
- sought to break the polarisation between the ruling and opposition parties
- Improves the quality of parliamentary
debates by bringing alternative voices to the Parliament as NMPs are experts in their field

- NMPs can argue and reason in parliamentary
debates without having to be bound to their political party's control

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
Front: Criticism about NMP scheme and independence
Back:
- Development in the last 20 years is that
there are functional constituencies and from whom NMPs are appointed
- They are functional, some of them seem to
think that their job is to articulate the concerns of their particular group
- The idea of the NMPs was independence and once
you have a functional NMP, it compromises his independence because then he has
to represent what the group says and how does he find out what the group says,
when he has not been chosen by said group

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
Back:
- Initially named ‘Council of State’, it was
renamed to the Presidential Council for Minority Rights in 1973
- The PCMR is an advisory body that:
considers all proposed legislation and report on whether the legislation
unfairly discriminates against a certain race to the Parliament
- It draws the parliament's attention to any bill
or subsidiary legislation that is a “differentiating measure”, that is
disadvantageous to persons of any racial or religious community

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
Front: What is the PCMR's work scope?
Back:
Have to vet all bills/subsidiary legislation except
- supply bills
- bills presented on a certificate of urgency
- defence bills

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
Back:
Extremely limited discretionary powers, largely ceremonial role.
powers:
- appointing PM
- declaring office of PM vacant
- withhold assent to dissolve parliament
- right to refuse assent to any bill that would draw down on SG's financial reserves
- right to refuse assent to any key civil service appointment listed in the Constitution
- to withhold concurrence for the continued detention of persons under SG's detention laws
- issue of prohibition orders under maintenance of religious harmony act in 1990

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
Front: What is the rationale behind having a President?
Back:
- Effective check on an over-strong govt given PAP's dominance
- safeguard on past reserves

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
Back:
- Introduction of Bill
- Debating of Bill
- First Reading
- Second Reading
- Third Reading
- PCMR
- Presidential assent
- Subsidiary legislation

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
Back:
- any MP may initiate the bill
- urgent bills could be read 3x and passed within a single day: certificate of urgency signed by President
- Permanent secretary of ministry sends draft bill to AGC, AGC vet and sent to MinLaw for approval before submission to Cabinet

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
Back:
1st reading: any member may introduce a bill provided sufficient notice is given to the House - 2 clear days for govt bills and 4 clear days for private member's bill. No questions

2nd reading:
Bill is circulated amongst members at least 10 clear days beforehand. Minister gives speech on objective of bill, debate. Bill is committed to the Committee of the Full House if it passes the second reading.

Committee stage where select committee must list findings and recommendations in a Select Committee report. OR committee of the whole house deliberates in great detail.

report stage where committee will present its findings to parliament.

3rd reading (after the House accepts the amended bill):
- more limited debate
- errors amended
- bill is put to a vote, will be passed by parliament if accepted
PCMR:
- Council must make a report to the speaker within 30 days
- no report means no differentiating measure
- if council issues an adverse report, parliament can either amend and resubmit or president assent with 2/3 majority
Once president assents, it becomes a law. the Act comes into force only at the date of its publication in the govt gazette. Note that publication date and its commencement date are 2 different things.

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
Back: Minister can only promulgate legislation that is within the powers of the primary enabling statute. Also subject to scrutiny by PCMR.

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
Front: How is the judiciary independent from other branches?
Back:
1)
SC judges have security of tenure, and can only be
dismissed by incapacity or gross misconduct
Exceptions: Supernumerary (“contract”) judges and
Judicial commissioners. JCs are appointed on temporary basis between 6 months
and 3 years.

2)
Remuneration: Judge’s pay cannot be adjusted after
appointment.

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
Front: How do the 3 branches (executive, legislature and judiciary) check one another?
Back:
·
Executive checked by
legislature (actions are subject to scrutiny in Parliament)

·
Executive checked by
president (appointment of KAH subject to president approval)

·
Legislature checked by
president (President must assent bills before they are passed)

·
President checked by
legislature (Can be vetoed by 2/3 majority in Parliament)

·
Judiciary checked by
President (SC Judges and CJ appointed by president on Cabinet’s advice.
President can prevent courts from considering validity of administrative acts
on the basis of ISA)

·
Executive and
Legislative checked by

Judiciary through
judicial review. Judiciary can examine administrative decisions and laws made.
